sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Hel** (*hel*) — Death, Underworld, Souls · Hidden One — is the daughter of [[loki|Loki]] and the giantess [[angrboda|Angrboða]], sister to the wolf [[fenrir|Fenrir]] and the serpent [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]], whom [[odinn|Óðinn]] cast down into [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]] and set over the dead: those who die of sickness and of old age are sent to her, and she apportions their dwellings in nine worlds.[^1]

Her hall is Éljúðnir, her dish Hunger and her knife Famine, her threshold Plunging to Destruction and her bed the Sick-bed hung with Gleaming Bale; she herself is half blue-black and half the colour of living flesh — 'easily recognized', Snorri says, downcast and fierce.[^1] Her one great scene is the hinge of the [[baldr|Baldr]] tragedy: when [[hermod|Hermóðr]] rides nine nights to ransom the dead god, it is Hel who sets the condition on which everything turns — if all things in the world weep for Baldr, he may return.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Hel**. The normalized Old Norse form is already plain ASCII — three letters and a capital, with no diacritic or distinctive letter for the restoration to recover — and so the name is Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule: the ASCII form loses nothing. This temple is domain-less: **hel.com** is a plain-ASCII address registered decades ago and is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection, watched for release; the project owns no form of this name and claims none.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34 (Loki's children; Hel cast into Niflheimr; the hall and its fittings; her appearance), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49 (Hermóðr's errand and Hel's condition), trans. Faulkes (1987).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Hel.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Hel** — at once the goddess's name and the common noun *hel* 'death, the grave, the realm of the dead'. It descends from Proto-Germanic *haljō*, formed on the verb *helan* / *heljan* 'to conceal, to cover': the hidden thing, and so 'the hidden one'.[^1] The lexicon glosses the meaning accordingly as 'Hidden one (from *heljan)'. The word is pan-Germanic: Gothic *halja* appears already in Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible translation, and Old English *helle* and Old High German *hella* continue it as the place of the dead.[^2]

A genuine scholarly debate attaches to the name, and this edition registers it honestly. The continental languages attest the *realm* everywhere and the *goddess* nowhere; Jacob Grimm reconstructed a continental goddess *Halja, but modern handbooks (Simek, Lindow) leave open whether Hel the person is an old deity or a Scandinavian personification of the older grave-word — the hidden place given a face.[^3] The lexicon's etymology itself is not in dispute: the derivation from *heljan* 'to conceal' is secure.

Because the normalized form is pure ASCII, the letter-by-letter transformation is the shortest in the Norse catalogue:

- **h** → **H** — Same, capitalized
- **e** → **e** — Same
- **l** → **l** — Same

Only the capitalization changes. The name is classified Tier 2 by the mechanical rule — the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses — which says something about the orthography and nothing about the goddess. The plain-ASCII address **hel.com** is held by a third party outside the collection and watched for release; this temple claims no domain.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. hel, Hel, helja.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Hel, hel; Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Hel.

Hel; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hel; Grimm, Jacob, Teutonic Mythology, trans. James Steven Stallybrass, 4 vols. (London: George Bell, 1882–88).

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈhel/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **H-** — Voiceless glottal fricative [h], fully sounded as in English *hall*
- **-e-** — Short close-mid front vowel [e], held brief; the short e of the verb *heljan*, not a long é
- **-l** — Single clear alveolar lateral [l]; the manuscripts write one l and the name keeps it light

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'HEL' — one crisp syllable, a short bright 'e' as in *get*, a single clean l. The English word *hell* is the name's own descendant and nearly its own pronunciation.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Hel, the goddess and the realm; the common noun *hel* 'death, the grave'
- **Gothic** — halja, the underworld-word of Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible[^2]
- **Old English / Old High German** — helle / hella, the realm kept without the goddess
- **Proto-Germanic** — *haljō, from *helan / *heljan* 'to conceal, to cover'

Hel is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing ASCII loses: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no vowel length. Three plain letters carry the whole underworld.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Hel.

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Hel** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda and the early codices of Snorri's Edda, recording material centuries older.[^1] The word's deeper attestation is Germanic-wide: Gothic *halja* stands already in Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible translation.

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- The form is *Hel*, a feminine noun from Proto-Germanic *haljō*, built on the verb *helan* / *heljan* 'to conceal, to cover' — hence 'hidden one / concealment'.[^2]
- Old Norse writes three plain Latin letters; there is no vowel length, diacritic, or distinctive letter for a Unicode restoration to recover, which is why the name is Tier 2 by the project's mechanical rule.
- In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛁᛚ (h-i-l, the ᛁ-rune covering e), though no runic attestation of the theonym survives.
- The plain-ASCII domain **hel.com** is held by a third party outside the PuniCodex collection and is watched for release; no form of the name is owned, and this temple claims none.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. hel, helja; de Vries, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (1962), s.v. Hel.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Hel** is catalogued under the domain Death, Underworld, Souls — the keeper of the dead who do not fall in battle, and the ruler of the place that shares her name.[^1]

### The Unheroic Dead

Óðinn's grant to her is explicit: she apportions dwellings to all who are sent to her — 'and those are the sickness-dead and the age-dead'. Where [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s Valhǫll selects the spectacular few, Hel receives the ordinary majority of humankind.

### The Underworld

Her realm lies beneath one root of [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]] (Grímnismál 31), and the corpus layers it downward: Óðinn boasts of travelling the nine worlds below Niflhel, 'thither men die out of Hel' (Vafþrúðnismál 43). The hidden one is hidden under the world's own structure.[^2]

### The Boundary

The road to her is measured in the [[hermod|Hermóðr]] myth — nine nights through dark valleys, the river Gjǫll, the gold-thatched bridge, the barred gate Helgrindr. What crosses in does not cross out: 'let Hel hold what she has' is her realm's whole charter.[^3]

### Loki's House

She is the daughter of [[loki|Loki]] and [[angrboda|Angrboða]], sister of [[fenrir|Fenrir]] and [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]] — the three children the gods could not kill and could only dispose of: the sea, the fetter, and the grave.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34, trans. Faulkes (1987).
The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014): Vafþrúðnismál 43; Grímnismál 31.
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
Hel's iconography is an inventory: Gylfaginning 34 furnishes her hall with named fittings that do the work a cult statue never did — the attributes are household objects, and each is named for what it takes away.[^1]

- **The half-blue, half-flesh face** — half blue-black, half the colour of living flesh: the two states of being divided by a single line, making her 'easily recognized'
- **Éljúðnir** — her hall, 'Sprayed with Snowstorms', behind high walls and great gates: architecture for the ordinary ending
- **Hungr and Sultr** — her dish Hunger, her knife Famine: the table-service of the wasting deaths she rules
- **Fallanda Forað** — 'Plunging to Destruction', the threshold of her bedchamber
- **Kǫr and Blíkjanda Bǫl** — her bed, the Sick-bed, and its hangings, Gleaming Bale: the dead received as the sick are received to bed
- **Ganglati and Ganglǫt** — her serving-man and serving-maid, both named for the slow walk: time in Hel moves at a dying pace[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hel.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Hel's mythology is an origin, a judgment, and a standing geography: she acts rarely and presides always.

### The Casting Down (Gylfaginning 34)

[[loki|Loki]] got three children on the giantess [[angrboda|Angrboða]]: the wolf [[fenrir|Fenrir]], the serpent [[jormungandr|Jǫrmungandr]], and Hel. When the gods learned the brood was being raised and read in prophecy that great harm would come of it, [[odinn|Óðinn]] disposed of each: the serpent into the encircling sea, the wolf kept among the Æsir to be bound, and Hel cast down into [[niflheimr|Niflheimr]] with authority over nine worlds — to apportion dwellings among those sent to her, the sickness-dead and the age-dead. Snorri then gives the inventory: the hall Éljúðnir, the dish Hunger and knife Famine, the slow-walking servants, the threshold Plunging to Destruction, the bed Sick-bed hung with Gleaming Bale — and the goddess herself, half blue-black and half flesh-coloured, downcast and fierce.[^1]

### The Weeping Condition (Gylfaginning 49)

When [[baldr|Baldr]] lay dead and [[hermod|Hermóðr]] had ridden the nine nights, leapt Helgrindr on [[sleipnir|Sleipnir]], and found his brother in the hall's high seat, he asked Hel for Baldr's release. Her answer is her only speech in the corpus, and the end of the world turns on it: if all things, living and lifeless, weep for Baldr, he shall return; if anything refuses, he stays with Hel. All things wept — men and beasts, earth and stones, trees and metals — until one giantess in a cave, calling herself Þökk, wept dry tears: 'let Hel hold what she has.' The gods suspected Þökk was Loki in disguise. Baldr stayed.[^2]

### The Strewn Benches (Baldrs draumar)

Before the fall, Óðinn himself rode down to a grave-mound east of Hel's gate and woke a dead völva, who told him for whom the realm was dressed: the benches strewn with arm-rings, the mead brewed, the shields overspread — for Baldr. The poem's glimpse inside the hall is the other side of Snorri's famine inventory: Hel's house is also a hall of honour, prepared in advance and shining, for the guest it expects.[^3]

### The Geography (Vafþrúðnismál 43; Grímnismál 31)

The Poetic Edda keeps her realm on the map: Óðinn's proof of far travel is that he passed through nine worlds below Niflhel, 'thither men die out of Hel'; and Grímnismál plants Hel's dwelling beneath one of the three roots of [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]]. The dead are not elsewhere — they are under the same tree, at another root.[^4]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
The Poetic Edda, trans. Larrington (2014): Vafþrúðnismál 43; Grímnismál 31.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The oldest syncretism is the one the sources perform on themselves: Saxo Grammaticus, writing Latin for a Danish court a generation before Snorri's Edda reached its final form, cannot say 'Hel' and so writes *Proserpina* — in Gesta Danorum Book 1 the goddess appears to Balderus in a dream as Proserpina, promising the dead man her embraces, the interpretatio latina folded directly into the plot.[^1] The same book sends the hero Hading under the earth, past a river crossed by a bridge, in a journey whose geography matches the Norse Hel-road.

The Greek comparison runs deeper than the name-swap: like Hades, Hel is both a person and a place — one goes *til Heljar*, to Hel, as one goes to Hades — and scholars since Grimm have asked whether the person is as old as the place. Grimm projected a continental goddess *Halja* backward from the Gothic and Old High German words; current scholarship (Simek, Lindow) is cooler, noting that the continent attests the realm but never the ruler, and leaving open whether the goddess is a Scandinavian personification of the grave-word.[^2]

The largest syncretism is the one history performed unasked: Christianity took the word itself and made it 'hell', the punitive fire of the damned — recolouring the goddess's quiet hall of the sick-dead into the most feared address in the language. Her name survived by being emptied of her.[^3]

sources.citation: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 1 (Proserpina's promise to Balderus; Hading's underworld journey), trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979).
Grimm, Jacob, Teutonic Mythology, trans. Stallybrass (1882–88); Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), s.v. Hel; Lindow, Norse Mythology: A Guide (2001), s.v. Hel.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (1957), s.v. hel.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Hel's afterlife is the English language's own: every speaker of English, German, or the Scandinavian tongues pronounces her name each time they say *hell* — the commonest relic any Norse deity has left behind, carried out of the temple and into the swear-word. The word's journey is her biography in reverse: the goddess faded, the place-name endured, and the place darkened from a hall of the age-dead into a prison of fire.[^1]

Modern reception has restored the person, if not the theology. She returns in Victorian and twentieth-century mythography, in Neil Gaiman's *Norse Mythology* (2017), and most visibly in Marvel's Hela, whose shadowed iconography reaches back past the comics to Snorri's two-coloured face.[^2] In modern Heathen and Ásatrú practice she is kept as the keeper of the ordinary ancestors — the goddess for everyone who will not die in battle, which is to say for nearly everyone — and the Baldr rites of the revival keep her single line of dialogue at the centre of the year's grief-cycle.[^3]

sources.citation: Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (1957), s.v. hel; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (1910), s.v. Hel.
Gaiman, Neil, Norse Mythology (London: Bloomsbury, 2017).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hel.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
Hel is a textual figure: no runestone invokes her, no votive deposit names her, and no Scandinavian place-name can be securely tied to her cult — a silence she shares with the corpus's whole chthonic stratum.[^1] Her attestation is manuscript evidence: the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Vafþrúðnismál, Grímnismál), the fourteenth-century AM 748 I 4to that alone preserves Baldrs draumar, and the early codices of Snorri's Edda, composed about 1220.

The word beneath her is far better attested than the goddess: Gothic *halja* appears in Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible translation, and Old English *helle* and Old High German *hella* fill the continental record as the name of the dead's place — but nowhere outside Scandinavia does the place carry a person.[^2] That distribution is itself the central datum in the debate over whether Hel is an old goddess or a late personification of the grave-word, a question Simek and Lindow keep open. Saxo's Proserpina in Gesta Danorum Book 1 is the nearest thing to an independent witness: a Danish historian already translating her for Latin readers before Snorri's Edda took its final shape.[^3]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hel.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Hel.
Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 1, trans. Fisher, ed. Davidson (1979).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic Edda knows Hel chiefly as geography and expectation rather than as an actress. *Grímnismál* 31 plants her beneath the world-tree: three roots hold [[yggdrasill|Yggdrasill]], and Hel dwells under one, men under another, the frost-giants under the third — the dead housed in the cosmos's own foundations.[^1] *Vafþrúðnismál* 43 folds the realm downward: Óðinn's proof that he has travelled farther than any god is that he passed through nine worlds below Niflhel — 'thither men die out of Hel', a death beneath death for those already dead.[^1]

*Baldrs draumar* gives the corpus's one look inside the hall before the [[baldr|Baldr]] tragedy: Óðinn rides down, wakes the völva at her grave-mound east of Hel's gate, and hears that the benches are strewn with arm-rings, the mead brewed, the shields overspread — for Baldr. The deadliest hospitality in the Edda is prepared in advance, and it is beautiful.[^2] *Vǫluspá* supplies the surrounding underworld — the hall on Nástrǫnd woven of serpent-backs for the oath-breakers — without naming the goddess herself: the poem's geography of punishment and keeping belongs to her realm whether or not her name is spoken.[^3]

sources.citation: The Poetic Edda, trans. Carolyne Larrington, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014): Grímnismál 31; Vafþrúðnismál 43.
Baldrs draumar (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
The Prose Edda is Hel's great witness — her origin, her portrait, her household, and her only speech all stand in Gylfaginning. Chapter 34 casts her down: Snorri names her father [[loki|Loki]] and mother [[angrboda|Angrboða]], records Óðinn's grant of authority over nine worlds and over the sickness-dead and age-dead, and then gives the inventory unmatched in the corpus — the hall Éljúðnir, the dish Hunger and knife Famine, the servants Ganglati and Ganglǫt, the threshold Plunging to Destruction, the bed Sick-bed with hangings Gleaming Bale — closing with the portrait: half blue-black, half the colour of living flesh, 'easily recognized, rather downcast and fierce of countenance'.[^1]

Chapter 49 gives her the scene on which the world's ending turns. [[hermod|Hermóðr]] leaps Helgrindr, finds [[baldr|Baldr]] in the high seat, and asks for his release; Hel answers with the condition of universal weeping — a test, she says, of whether Baldr is as beloved as is said. The condition fails by one refusal, and Snorri's dry closing note — that the gods believed Þökk was Loki in another shape — leaves Hel blameless at the hinge of the tragedy: she offered terms, and the world could not meet them.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 49, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The runic corpus contains no invocation of the goddess Hel. No runestone asks her favour, no amulet bears her name, and no inscription links a dedicant to her keeping — a silence consistent with her character as the receiver of the uncommemorated dead rather than a deity of cult dedication.[^1]

The word beneath her is older than any runestone that could have carried it: Gothic *halja* is attested in Ulfilas's fourth-century Bible, and the continental reflexes (Old English *helle*, Old High German *hella*) are literary before they are epigraphic. In the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚼᛁᛚ (h-i-l, the ᛁ-rune covering e), but no such carving of the theonym survives; the manuscript record is the primary witness, and the epigraphic silence is itself part of the personification debate the handbooks keep open.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Hel.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Hel; Simek, Dictionary of Northern Mythology (1993), s.v. Hel.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
Beyond the Eddas, Hel's medieval afterlife runs through Saxo Grammaticus's Latin. In Gesta Danorum Book 1, the goddess appears to the dreaming Balderus as *Proserpina*, promising him her embraces — the interpretatio latina not as a scholar's footnote but as a plot event, and the clearest proof that the Baldr cycle carried the death-goddess into Danish historiography a generation before Snorri's Edda took its final form.[^1] The same book sends the hero Hading beneath the earth with a mysterious woman, past a river spanned by a bridge where two armies fight without end — an underworld journey whose geography matches the Norse Hel-road of the [[hermod|Hermóðr]] myth.[^1]

In the Icelandic saga record she is present chiefly as the common noun: men 'go to Hel' (*fara til Heljar*) across the family sagas as they go to the grave, the goddess absorbed into the idiom of ordinary dying. The distribution is the datum: Scandinavia kept both the word and the woman; the continent kept only the word.[^2]

sources.citation: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 1, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (1957), s.v. hel (fara til heljar and kindred idioms).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Hel is what the gods do with what they cannot destroy. Óðinn cannot kill Loki's daughter — the prophecies forbid the thought — so he hides her, and the hiding is so thorough that it becomes an office: the concealed one becomes the keeper of everyone else the world conceals. Her name says it plainly: the hidden one, from the verb for covering over.[^1]

And her charter is more honest than Valhǫll's. Óðinn's hall takes the spectacular few, the spear-marked and the chosen; Hel takes the rest — the sick, the old, the farmers in their beds — which is to say she receives, in the end, almost the whole of humankind, and keeps it behind a gate no god has ever forced. 'Let Hel hold what she has' was meant as a curse.[^2] It is also simply the truth of things, and the Edda knew it: everything that dies quietly is already hers, and she has never once given it back.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 34, trans. Faulkes (1987); Cleasby & Vigfússon, s.v. helja.
